claims.text: A targeted post-synthesis thermal annealing treatment will increase the coercive field of a magnetic high-entropy alloy.
Thermal annealing can induce controlled nanoscale precipitate formation in the target magnetic HEA.
Nanoscale precipitates provide additional domain-wall pinning sites.
The proposed initial material is an as-cast or rapidly solidified, single-phase magnetic HEA with homogeneous elemental distribution and minimal nanoscale segregation or precipitates.
An annealing temperature around 1023 K is near the onset of elemental segregation and is motivated by relevant temperature regimes in refractory HEAs.
The annealing treatment is expected to produce precipitates such as Cr/V-rich clusters.
The coercivity-enhancing effect should apply to magnetic HEAs with BCC or FCC structures that contain elements prone to phase separation.
Precipitates on the order of a few nanometers are required for the beneficial coercivity effect.
Excessive grain growth or precipitate coalescence must be avoided for the coercivity increase to occur.
Annealing under an inert atmosphere is necessary to prevent oxidation.
The relevant nanoscale precipitates or segregated clusters should preferably be located at grain boundaries or triple junctions.
Nanoscale precipitates obstruct domain-wall motion during magnetization reversal.
The barrier to domain-wall movement produced by precipitates increases the coercive field.
The annealed alloy will have a higher coercive field than an otherwise matched as-cast alloy.
A homogeneous untreated magnetic HEA has lower coercivity because it lacks effective domain-wall-pinning features.
Precipitates that are too large or too sparse may fail to increase coercivity.
Deleterious phase changes caused by annealing may prevent the predicted coercivity increase.
